name: Makassar Malay / Makassarese Malay, i.e. 'local Indonesian' of Makassar
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Jukes, Anthony. 2006. Makassarese (basa Mangkasara'): a description of an Austronesian language of South Sulawesi. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics and Applied Linguistics, University of Melbourne. Open PDF athttp://www.oxis.org/theses/jukes-2006.pdf.
catalog_locator: Ch. 1, sec. 1.3.2.1 'Malay/Indonesian', pp. 37-38. Makassarese proper: sec. 2.2.3 'Stress', pp. 91-92.
catalog_quote: In modern Makassar it is not clear that Makassar Malay as such can adequately be differentiated from code-switching and code-mixing between Malay/Indonesian and Makassarese. According to Tadmor (2003) “many bilingual speakers possess basically one grammatical structure, and when speaking Malay/Indonesian, they simply ʻgraftʼ Malay morphemes onto the Makassarese structure, and produce them with Makassarese phonology. In the speech of some younger speakers, who do not speak Makassarese, this strong interference has now become a substratum”. Specifically, Makassarese influence on local Indonesian can be seen in the following tendencies: • replacement of all final nasals with velar nasal • replacement of schwa with /a/ • Makassarese stress patterns (strong penultimate stress) — this is the most obvious characteristic of the Makassarese or South Sulawesi accent of Indonesian • the use of Makassarese clitics, especially aspectuals =mo, =pa etc
world_status: statement found in an open source

Specifically, Makassarese influence on local Indonesian can be seen in the following tendencies: - replacement of all final nasals with velar nasal - replacement of schwa with /a/[fn 24] - Makassarese stress patterns (strong penultimate stress) - this is the most obvious characteristic of the Makass…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Makassar Malay / Makassar Indonesian carries over the Makassarese stress pattern: strong stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (Makassarese itself has regular penultimate word stress per the same thesis, ch. 2). Since schwa is replaced by /a/, the Standard-Malay schwa-penult exception presumably does not arise, but the source does not say so explicitly.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for the Malay variety.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned for the Malay variety; the remark is a one-line characterization, not a rule statement with exceptions (whether Makassarese clitics such as =mo, =pa fall outside the stress window, as they do in Makassarese, is not stated for Makassar Malay).
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic remark about the 'accent' of local Indonesian; word-level penultimate stress implied by 'Makassarese stress patterns', no discussion of phrase vs word domain or citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is about 'local Indonesian' / 'the modern variety of Bahasa Indonesia spoken in Makassar', which Jukes (2006: 37) explicitly lists as one of the three referents of the label 'Makassar Malay'; this matches Glottolog maka1305 = Ethnologue mfp 'Indonesian, Makassar'. The statement sits inside a grammar of Makassarese (maka1311, the substrate language, itself regular penultimate stress per Jukes 2006 ch. 2) and attributes the Malay variety's stress to Makassarese transfer; it is not a phonological description of Makassar Malay in its own right.
